common_name: Coppertina Ninebark (Copper-Orange New Growth Foliage Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Coppertina emerges bright coppery-orange in spring, deepening to burgundy-red as the foliage matures through summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Coppertina stands out among dark-leaved ninebarks for its color-shifting foliage, emerging a vivid coppery-orange in spring before deepening to a rich burgundy-red through summer, a warmer tone than the near-black purple of Diabolo, with clusters of small white-to-pink flowers in late spring followed by reddish seed capsules and exfoliating bark for winter interest. Full sun brings out the most vivid color contrast between new and mature growth, while shadier sites mute the effect. It tolerates a wide range of soil conditions and needs only occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems at the base each year to keep the shrub full and encourage the brightest new copper growth.

common_name: Ginger Wine Ninebark (Copper-to-Burgundy Foliage Compact Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Ginger Wine is a more compact ninebark than older cultivars like Diabolo, fitting smaller mixed borders and foundation plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Ginger Wine bears warm ginger-copper new growth that deepens toward burgundy-wine as leaves mature, giving a two-toned effect across the shrub through the growing season, on a more compact, rounded frame than older, larger-growing dark-leaved ninebark cultivars. Small clusters of white-to-pink flowers appear in late spring, followed by reddish seed capsules, and mature stems develop the characteristic exfoliating bark that adds winter interest. Full sun produces the richest foliage color. It needs only occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems at the base every year or two to keep the shrub full and vigorous.

common_name: Dart's Gold Ninebark (Classic Golden-Yellow Foliage Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Dart's Gold is one of the original golden-foliage ninebark cultivars and can scorch in the hottest, most exposed full-sun sites without adequate soil moisture.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; some afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in hot climates while still keeping the foliage bright gold rather than fading to green. Dart's Gold is a longtime classic among golden-leaved shrubs, producing bright chartreuse-yellow foliage that holds its color through the growing season, contrasting well with dark-leaved companions like Diabolo ninebark or purple-leaved smokebush, and small clusters of white-to-pink flowers appear in late spring followed by reddish seed capsules. Mature stems develop the characteristic peeling, multi-layered bark that gives ninebark its common name, adding winter interest once the leaves drop. It tolerates a wide range of soil conditions, including clay and periodic flooding, and needs only occasional renewal pruning to remove old stems at the base and keep the shrub full.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Rubidor pairs bright golden-yellow foliage with red-throated pink flowers, a bolder color combination than the more common purple- or green-leaved weigela cultivars.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; some afternoon shade in hot climates helps prevent leaf scorch while the golden foliage still colors up well. Rubidor produces bright, sunny yellow-gold leaves through the growing season, a striking backdrop for the funnel-shaped, deep pink flowers with a contrasting red throat that open in a heavy flush in late spring, with scattered rebloom through summer. Its bold foliage color makes it a strong accent or focal shrub even when not in flower, pairing well with purple- or burgundy-leaved companions for contrast. Prune right after the main spring bloom to shape the plant and encourage branching for the next season's flowers, since weigela sets buds on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Polka reblooms through summer on new growth rather than flowering only once in spring like older weigela cultivars.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; good drainage helps prevent the root problems weigela can develop in heavy, waterlogged soil. Polka is a Polish-bred reblooming weigela that covers itself in funnel-shaped, rich pink flowers in a heavy late-spring flush, then continues producing scattered flowers on new growth through summer into fall, giving a much longer season of color than older single-flush weigela cultivars. Its compact, rounded habit fits smaller mixed borders and foundation plantings without the sprawling size of older weigela varieties. Deadhead spent flower clusters lightly to encourage continued rebloom, and prune immediately after the main spring flush if size reduction is needed, since it still sets some buds on year-old wood in addition to blooming on new growth.
